data.title: Lake - Water Level Monitoring LIVE
data.description: Smiths Lake Water Level — Live & Free - tells you things you need to know before the sandbar opens.
data.notes: When heavy rain sets in, combined with high water levels, one question dominates the village: how full is the lake, and is it heading for an opening?  The answer is available online, in real time, around the clock — and many residents and most visitors don't know it exists.
data.projhubAboutContent:
Smiths Lake is monitored 24 hours a day, seven days a week, by Manly Hydraulics Laboratory (MHL) under a NSW Government contracted program of waterways monitoring and measurement.  The gauge station is located at Tarbuck Bay, and the live reading — in metres Above Mean Sea Level (AMSL) — is publicly accessible online at any time, free of charge.
Different members of the community watch the lake level for different reasons:
• Boat owners need time to move vessels before the sandbar opens
• Foreshore property owners monitor for flood risk
• Fishermen plan around the timing of an opening
• Holiday-makers want to know what the lake will look like on arrival
The Opening Trigger
The trigger level for an opening is 2.1m AMSL, adjusted up or down depending on forecast weather conditions.  MidCoast Council monitors the gauge closely as the water approaches this level and coordinates with the Bureau of Meteorology before any decision is made.
The Reading is Free and Always On
Real-time water level data is publicly available, updated continuously, and free of charge.  No registration, no app, no subscription — just a live number, updated around the clock.
🌊 View the live Smiths Lake water level at mhl.nsw.gov.au/Site-209465 — Tarbuck Bay, Site 209465.  Real-time data, updated continuously.
📄 Historical lake level data is also available in our Documents section.

data.title: Lake Opening - Recent & Historical
data.description: The lake has been opened to the ocean periodically since 1932 — to protect low-lying properties and improve water quality.  Lake levels are publicly monitored.
data.projhubAboutContent:
Smiths Lake has been mechanically opened to the ocean periodically since 1932, to prevent inundation of low-lying properties and improve water quality.

When open to the ocean, the lake is subject to ocean tides, swell, and currents.  When closed, the main source of water flowing into the lake is a network of small creeks, including Wamwarra and Tarbuck.

Lake levels are monitored by Manly Hydraulics Laboratory, and current and historical records are publicly available.

data.title: Did Smiths Lake Once Have Fruit Plantations? 1901
data.description:
Did Smiths Lake Once Have Fruit Plantations?
We're searching for a piece of our local history that hasn't yet made it into the written record.
Community memory suggests there may have been banana and/or passionfruit cultivation in the Smiths Lake area — possibly on farms run by some of our earliest settler families. But so far, we haven't been able to confirm it from historical documents or archives.
data.notes:
Did Smiths Lake Once Have Fruit Plantations?
If your family has a connection to fruit farming here — or if you remember hearing stories from older residents — we'd love to hear from you.
We're particularly hoping someone can tell us:
• Which families farmed fruit in the area, and when
• Where the plantations were located
• What happened to them
And we'd be thrilled if anyone has photographs.
Old photos of farming life around Smiths Lake — of any kind, not just fruit farms — are a treasure. If you have images tucked away in an album or on an old hard drive, please reach out. With your permission, we'd love to share them here as part of our growing History section.
📩 Contact us via the feedback form — or speak to any PPCA subcommittee member.
Every family story, every old photo, every 'I remember my grandfather saying...' helps build the picture. Nothing is too small.

data.description: Six tonnes and counting.  Rubbish, derelict craft and abandoned equipment — gone.
data.notes: Over four annual Clean-Up Days, Smiths Lake Village volunteers have removed more than six tonnes of derelict craft and rubbish from the village foreshore and green spaces. Here is what we have achieved together.
data.projhubAboutContent:
Our volunteer Clean-Up Day program focuses on the Smiths Lake Village foreshore, green spaces, and surrounding precinct areas. Supported by Clean Up Australia, the program provides free disposal of all collected waste at the MidCoast Recycling Centre.
Over four annual events, volunteers have removed and disposed of more than six tonnes of derelict craft and rubbish from the village foreshore and green spaces — a remarkable achievement by a dedicated community.
Our most recent event, held Sunday 8 March 2026, retrieved 1.06 tonnes of rubbish and abandoned equipment from the lakeside foreshore along Sandbar Road, transported to the Tuncurry Recycling Centre.
Every year the foreshore looks better for it. Thank you to everyone who has rolled up their sleeves and helped make it happen.

data.title: Lake - Openings, Recent & Historical
data.description: Smiths Lake is what scientists classify as an intermittently closed and open lake (ICOLL) — a coastal lagoon that is predominantly closed to the ocean, but periodically opened, either naturally or mechanically, to manage water levels and maintain the health of the estuary.
data.projhubAboutContent:
Smiths Lake has been mechanically opened to the ocean periodically, since 1932 to prevent inundation of low-lying properties and improve water quality.  When open to the ocean, the lake is subject to ocean tides, swell and
currents.  When closed to the ocean, the main source of water flowing into the lake is
from a network of small creeks including Wamwarra and Tarbuck creeks.  Lake levels are monitored by Manly Hydraulics Laboratory.  Current and historical records are publicly available.

Smiths Lake High-Water Trail
A group of Smiths Lake Village residents is working to connect and enhance the existing informal trail network around the shores of Smiths Lake. The vision is simple: a low-impact, off-road pedestrian path that connects our favourite places and invites locals and visitors to explore and linger in the village, rather than travel elsewhere for bushwalking and recreation.
The High-Water Trail will showcase more of the area's natural beauty to a wider audience, support the local economy, and extend visitor activity beyond the peak season. It will also deliver practical benefits — enabling land care, weed management, and the removal of abandoned equipment and rubbish from the foreshore.
The trail serves a broad range of recreational users — bushwalkers, kayakers, and birdwatchers — united by a commitment to protecting and preserving Smiths Lake's unique natural environment while encouraging sustainable, minimal-impact access for all.

data.projhubFAQsContent:
Q.  What is AusAlert?
A.  AusAlert is Australia's new national emergency warning system, using cell-broadcast technology to send urgent messages directly to compatible mobile phones and devices within a specified area. The system enables emergency services and selected Australian Government agencies to deliver targeted warnings quickly and reliably — reaching people when it matters most, helping to save lives and property. AusAlert is more reliable, accurate, and efficient than existing warning systems.  In future, the system will also send automated voice messages to landline phones.
 
Q.  What will an AusAlert announce?
A.  An AusAlert message will tell you:
•  what the emergency is
•  where it is happening
•  how serious it is
•  what you should do
•  who the message is from
•  where to find more information.
 
Q.  When AusAlert may be used?
A.  AusAlert may be used for a range of situations, including:
•  Natural hazards, such as bushfires, floods, cyclones and tsunamis
•  Public safety and security threats, such as serious public safety incidents or terrorism
•  Biosecurity incidents, such as animal or plant disease and biohazard outbreaks
•  Health emergencies, such as pandemics or other national public health events.

data.projhubAboutContent:
The health of Smiths Lake and its waterways is monitored through complementary programs:
MidCoast Council Waterways Monitoring
MidCoast Council conducts a recurring program of waterways monitoring and measurement across the lake and surrounding catchment, with results compiled and reported by Council. Periodic testing is conducted throughout the year.
Joint Council and Community Water Quality Program
A joint committee of MidCoast Council representatives and community members conducts regular testing and monitoring of Smiths Lake water quality and waterways health. Parameters tested include pH, salinity, dissolved oxygen levels and algae presence — the key indicators of a healthy coastal lagoon.
Results are published as interactive Waterway and Catchment Report Cards, allowing residents and visitors to view current and historical readings at a glance.

data.title: Naming of Pacific Palms (1959)
data.description:
The Name 'Pacific Palms' was Invented in 1959 - The Story
The name 'Pacific Palms' — now the official address for Blueys Beach, Boomerang Beach, and the broader area — is not a historical geographical name of any antiquity.  It was deliberately coined by a local progress association in 1959, specifically to make the area sound more appealing to Sydney real estate buyers.  The name was chosen as part of Degotardi's broader marketing campaign — a deliberate rebranding of what had simply been known as the Smiths Lake district.

data.title: Lake - Water Level Monitoring
data.description: Smiths Lake Water Level — Live & Free
data.notes: When the rain sets in, one question dominates the village: how full is the lake, and is it heading for an opening? The answer is available online, in real time, around the clock - many residents, and most visitors, don't know it exists.
data.projhubAboutContent:
Smiths Lake is monitored 24 hours a day, seven days a week, by Manly Hydraulics Laboratory (MHL) under a NSW Government contracted program of waterways monitoring and measurement. The gauge station is located at Tarbuck Bay, and the live reading — in metres Above Mean Sea Level (AMSL) — is publicly accessible online at any time, free of charge.
When heavy rain arrives — summer storms, east coast lows, or a sustained wet spell — the lake level becomes one of the most watched numbers in the village. Different members of the community watch it for different reasons:
• Boat owners need time to move vessels before the sandbar opens
• Foreshore property owners monitor for flood risk
• Fishermen plan around the timing of an opening
• Holiday-makers want to know what the lake will look like on arrival
The trigger level for an opening is 2.1m AMSL, adjusted up or down depending on forecast weather conditions. MidCoast Council monitors the gauge closely as the water approaches this level and coordinates with the Bureau of Meteorology before any decision is made.
🌊 View the live Smiths Lake water level at mhl.nsw.gov.au/Site-209465 — Tarbuck Bay, Site 209465. Real-time data, updated continuously.
Historical lake level data is also available in our Documents section.

data.title: Worimi Heritage
data.description:
The Worimi People and Smiths Lake — A Story Being Developed.  
Smiths Lake sits at the heart of Worimi country.  For thousands of years before European arrival, this remarkable combination of coastal lagoon, ocean access, abundant fish, and surrounding forest made it one of the most productive and significant places in the Worimi world.
This is a story we are committed to telling well — and that means telling it in Worimi voices, with Worimi guidance.
We are currently working to develop this history in partnership with the Forster Local Aboriginal Land Council, and we look forward to sharing it here as that conversation grows.
We acknowledge the Worimi people as the traditional custodians of the land on which Smiths Lake Village is located, and pay our respects to Elders past, present and emerging.
data.notes:
What the Research Record Shows - 
The Worimi people are the traditional custodians of a country that extended from the Hunter River in the south to Forster in the north — encompassing Smiths Lake entirely. They spoke the Gathang language, which is undergoing active revival in the 21st century.
•  The Worimi nation's territory encompassed Smiths Lake within its cultural and geographic extent
•  In the area stretching from Wallis Lake to Newcastle, there are 37 recorded Ceremonial Sites (stone arrangements, bora grounds, carved trees, burial sites), 115 recorded campsites, and 97 middens documented
•  The Port Stephens–Great Lakes Marine Park explicitly recognises: 'Aboriginal people's association with the area's sea and land dates back thousands of years and local people still gather food in the traditional way'
•  The Worimi people view land and sea country as one living entity — rivers, creeks, wetlands, the ocean and all living species are interconnected parts of country
•  Many significant cultural and spiritual sites are located within or adjacent to the Marine Park, including middens, burial sites and traditional campsites
•  The ancient middens and carved trees found around the Smiths Lake area are visible evidence of this continuous connection
•  Today the Forster Local Aboriginal Land Council works with Worimi descendants to promote, foster and protect culture and heritage

data.title: Sustainability Programs
data.description: Your Backyard, Your Bushland.  Free workshops, citizen science, and hands-on programs — protecting what makes Smiths Lake special.
data.notes: MidCoast Council runs a suite of free sustainability programs for Smiths Lake residents — from backyard biodiversity to composting, native gardening and energy conservation.  Most require nothing more than a willingness to get involved.
data.projhubAboutContent:
Smiths Lake sits within some of the most ecologically significant bushland on the NSW mid-north coast.  The programs below are designed to help residents play an active role in protecting it — whether your backyard is a manicured garden, a bush block, or something in between.
Backyards for Biodiversity
Coordinated by MidCoast Council in partnership with National Parks and Wildlife, and supported by the NSW Government Environmental Trust, Backyards for Biodiversity is a practical program for anyone with plants on their property.  It focuses on two things: reducing the spread of invasive plants into native bushland, and making private gardens better habitat for local wildlife.
The program is designed for every kind of resident:
• The fastidious gardener wanting to know whether their garden is genuinely wildlife-friendly
• The weekend warrior ready to tackle the right weeds and introduce the right natives
• The gardening avoider who may not realise what is spreading beyond their fence line
Smiths Lake was selected for the current round of the program because of the exceptional bushland surrounding the village and the strong momentum already built by local volunteers, Council bush re-generators and National Parks.  Results so far have been significant.
Get Involved in the Science
Residents are invited to contribute to wildlife monitoring through the iNaturalist app.  Simply photograph or record plants and animals in your backyard, along the foreshore, or in the surrounding bushland and upload them to the Smiths Lake Biodiversity project via iNaturalist.  Every record helps build a clearer picture of what is living here.
The Yellow-bellied Glider
A particular focus of the current program is the Yellow-bellied Glider (Petaurus australis) — an endangered marsupial that inhabits the tall eucalypt forests around Smiths Lake.  If you have heard a loud, piercing shriek in the bush at night that turns into a rattle, audible up to 500 metres away, you have likely heard one.  Council has been working across 60 hectares of public reserves to protect glider habitat, including installation of artificial nesting hollows using Hollow Hog technology to compensate for the loss of mature hollow-bearing trees.  Camera monitoring has confirmed gliders are present and active in the area.
Free Sustainability Workshops
MidCoast Council runs periodic free workshops on sustainable living topics including composting, solar energy, water conservation, native gardening and reducing waste.  All materials are provided.  Registration is required — use the link below to register your interest via the feedback form.
Simple Things You Can Do Now
• Remove plants with the potential to invade bushland — the Garden Escapees weed handbook is a good starting point
• Plant a selection of local native species and add mulch, rocks, hollow logs or nest boxes to create habitat
• Install a pond or birdbath for birds, lizards and other wildlife
• Put green waste in the green bin or compost — never pile it in bushland
• Keep cats indoors or in a cat-run, particularly at night
📄 Program resources, newsletters and fact sheets are available in our Documents section, including the Smiths Lake Biodiversity overview, Wildlife-friendly Gardens guide and Yellow-bellied Glider fact sheet.
🔗 Register your interest in upcoming workshops via our feedback form.

Hunter New England and Central Coast Primary Health Network (HNECC PHN) — Health Insights Survey
HNECC PHN works to improve access to primary health care services across our region. The Health Insights Survey helps them understand the health needs, service gaps, and priorities of local communities. Results feed directly into HNECC PHN's official Needs Assessment report, provided to the Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing.

The full survey takes about 15 minutes. If you're short on time, the snapshot survey covers three open-text questions and takes under 5 minutes — it still feeds the same Needs Assessment.

You can complete either survey anonymously, or choose to provide your name and email at the end.
data.projhubFAQsContent:
Q: Is the survey anonymous?
A: Yes — you can complete it fully anonymously, or optionally provide your name and email at the end.

Q: How long does it take?
A: The full survey takes about 15 minutes. A shorter snapshot survey (three open-text questions) takes under 5 minutes.

Q: What happens with the results?
A: Results inform HNECC PHN's official Needs Assessment report to the Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, helping shape local health services and funding priorities.

Q: Is this a PPCA survey?
A: No — this is run directly by the Hunter New England and Central Coast Primary Health Network (HNECC PHN), an Australian Government-funded body. PPCA is sharing it to encourage Smiths Lake residents to have their say.
